title: If Only I Had Seen This Situation Before!
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece acknowledges that experience matters, since leaders who have faced a situation before can draw on proven tactics and focus on the people and issues that count. It then turns to the opposite case: leaders who face something new and conclude that their lack of experience will doom their performance. The article names this as a self-limiting belief that becomes self-fulfilling, causing leaders to avoid risks, pass on opportunities and forgo effective strategies. The best leaders, it argues, consciously refuse this line of thought and trust the creativity, intelligence and industry they bring to a novel situation. The closing move reframes experience itself as something only gained in retrospect, so learning by doing is the way forward.
points: Prior experience helps leaders because tactics from earlier episodes indicate what will and will not work, freeing attention for people and issues.
The belief that one lacks the necessary experience is identified as the most pernicious self-limiting belief for leaders, because it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Effective leaders make a conscious decision to rely on what they do know, including their creativity and smarts, rather than dwelling on what they do not.
Because the knowledge from experience is always gained in retrospect, the article argues the best learning often comes simply from acting.
quotes: Leaders who have seen a situation before feel more confident and better able to focus on the people and issues that count. Strategies and tactics employed in a previous episode give leaders a good idea of what will work in the current situation and what won’t.

Approaching a situation a leader has never before encountered can be a nerve-racking experience. Too often, leaders believe their lack of experience with a situation will undermine their ability to perform.
Leaders who hold this belief to an extreme underplay the creativity and smarts they bring to the table. Such a self-limited belief soon becomes a false accusation.

A self-limiting belief is a state of mind that constrains or restricts the ability to perform at the highest level. Such beliefs prevent leaders from taking risks, pursuing opportunities, and employing effective strategies in new situations.

The best leaders make a conscious decision not to fall prey to this self-fulfilling thought. They remind themselves that they possess the creativity, smarts, and industry to figure out how best to proceed in a new situation.
Rather than question what they don’t know regarding a situation, they rely on what they do know and engage accordingly. The knowledge we gain through experience is always in retrospect.
